title: Docker Production Best Practices
subtitle: Operating containers beyond a laptop
description: Production is a set of promises: reproducible artifacts, graceful failure, observable behaviour, safe configuration and tested recovery. This course turns Docker knowledge into operational discipline.
outcomes: Instrument, back up and recover a service

lessons.title: Production readiness checklist
lessons.summary: The non-negotiables that separate a demo from a service you can operate.
objectives: Evaluate an image and Compose stack against a readiness checklist

sections.title: Immutable artifacts, mutable configuration
sections.body:
Build once and promote the same image. Configuration comes from the environment, mounted files or a secret store. The image should not know whether it is in staging or production.

A production service must start without manual steps, expose a readiness signal, log to stdout, handle SIGTERM, bound its resource use, and fail safely when dependencies are unavailable.

sections.code:
# Graceful shutdown requires exec form and a signal-aware app
ENTRYPOINT ["node", "dist/server.js"]
STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM
sections.note: Node, Go, Python and Java all need explicit SIGTERM handling. Docker sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period.

sections.code:
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/acme/api@sha256:...
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: ["/tmp"]
    user: "10001:10001"
    cap_drop: ["ALL"]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "healthcheck.js"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
sections.note: A production Compose service should read like a policy document.

sections.title: Do not run a demo stack in production
sections.body: The default bridge network, no resource limits, `latest`, root user and no health checks are acceptable for a demo and unacceptable for a service.

exercises.title: Checklist audit
exercises.prompt: Audit a compose service against five readiness areas.
exercises.expected: Check image pinning, config, resources, health and security.

exercises.title: Graceful shutdown
exercises.prompt: Add a 30s stop grace period and a SIGTERM handler plan.

questions.question: What should change between staging and production?
questions.explain: The artifact stays identical; configuration changes.

questions.question: Why is exec-form ENTRYPOINT important in production?
questions.explain: Exec form avoids a shell masking PID 1 signals.

questions.question: Which is a production requirement for data?
questions.explain: Untested backups are not a recovery plan.

lessons.title: Production Compose
lessons.summary: A disciplined single-host deployment: pinned images, explicit policy, secrets, logging and resource limits.
objectives: Write a production Compose file and override
Pin images and control pull behaviour
Apply restart, logging and resource policy

sections.title: One host, explicit policy
sections.body: Compose is a legitimate production tool for single-host or small deployments when you accept its limits: no rescheduling, no multi-node failover, manual rolling updates. Write policy explicitly instead of relying on defaults.

sections.code:
name: acme
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/acme/api:1.4.0
    pull_policy: always
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:3000:3000"]
    env_file: [.env.production]
    secrets: [db_password]
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: ["/tmp"]
    cap_drop: ["ALL"]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { cpus: "1.5", memory: 512M }
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" }
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "healthcheck.js"]
      interval: 15s
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }

  db:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 10s

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: /etc/acme/db_password
volumes:
  pgdata:
    name: acme_pgdata
sections.note: Compose supports `deploy.resources.limits` on a single host even without Swarm.

sections.code:
docker compose -f compose.yaml config --quiet
docker compose -f compose.yaml pull
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --wait
docker compose -f compose.yaml ps
sections.note: Run from a versioned deployment directory, not from a developer checkout.

sections.title: Compose does not reschedule
sections.body: If the host dies, the service is down until you intervene. For HA, use an orchestrator or a managed platform.

lessons.title: Zero-downtime updates
lessons.summary: Rolling a service without dropping requests requires draining, health checks and a proxy that understands readiness.
objectives: Handle database migrations without breaking old code

sections.title: The update sequence
sections.body:
Start the new version, wait until it is healthy, add it to the proxy, then drain and stop the old version. Compose on a single host cannot do this for a published port by itself; put a reverse proxy in front and use two instances or an orchestrator.

Migrations must be backward compatible: add columns before code needs them, deploy code that writes both shapes, then remove the old shape. A destructive migration in the same release as the code is a downtime guarantee.

items.title: Build and push
items.body: Produce an immutable image and digest.

items.title: Start alongside
items.body: Run the new container on a different internal port.

items.title: Wait for readiness
items.body: Poll the readiness endpoint, not just the port.

items.title: Shift traffic
items.body: Update the proxy upstream and reload gracefully.

items.title: Drain and stop
items.body: Stop accepting new connections, wait for in-flight requests, then stop the old container.

sections.code:
# Caddy upstream switch (conceptual)
reverse_proxy /api/* api-blue:3000 api-green:3000 {
  lb_policy first
  health_uri /health/ready
  health_interval 5s
  fail_duration 30s
}
sections.note: In Compose, changing the proxy config and reloading is often the practical traffic switch. Swarm/Kubernetes automate this.

sections.title: A health check that only tests port 3000 is not readiness
sections.body: Check dependencies and warm-up state; otherwise traffic arrives before the app can serve it.

exercises.title: Blue/green plan
exercises.prompt: Describe a blue/green update for a Compose service behind Caddy.
exercises.expected: Run green on a new internal port, wait healthy, switch upstream, drain blue.

exercises.title: Safe migration
exercises.prompt: Write the three-step expand/contract migration sequence.
exercises.expected: Add new column nullable → deploy dual-write/read → remove old column later.

questions.question: What is the correct point to send traffic to a new container?
Why must migrations be backward compatible?
options: Old and new code run simultaneously
questions.explain: During rollout both versions may run.

questions.question: Can Compose alone do zero-downtime on one published port?
questions.explain: A single published port cannot overlap old and new containers.

lessons.title: Observability and SLOs
lessons.summary: Logs, metrics and traces are not decoration. They are how you know whether the service is keeping its promises.
objectives: Define SLIs and SLOs for a container service

sections.title: Start from user-visible behaviour
sections.body:
An SLI is a measured signal (request success rate, latency, saturation). An SLO is a target over a window. Dashboards should answer: are users succeeding, and how fast? Container CPU is a supporting signal, not the goal.

Use structured JSON logs with request IDs, stable metric names and trace propagation. Keep high-cardinality data out of metric labels.

sections.note: One line per event. Do not log secrets or request bodies by default.

sections.title: Alert on symptoms, page on burn rate
sections.body: A page for every CPU spike destroys trust. Alert when the error budget is burning or a user-visible SLO is at risk.

exercises.title: Define an SLI
exercises.prompt: Define success rate and p95 latency SLIs for an HTTP API.
exercises.expected: successful_requests/total_requests; p95 latency over a window.

exercises.title: Structured log
exercises.prompt: Write one JSON log line for a failed request.
exercises.expected: Include level, ts, service, requestId, route, status, durationMs, error.

questions.question: What is an SLO?
options: A target for a measured service-level indicator
questions.explain: It is an objective for reliability.

questions.question: Which label is dangerous in metrics?
What should logs contain?
questions.explain: Structured logs are queryable and correlatable.

lessons.title: Backup, restore and disaster recovery
lessons.summary: The recovery plan is the product. Everything else is a backup you hope works.
objectives: Design backups for data and configuration

sections.title: What must be recoverable
sections.body:
Application data (volumes or database dumps), secrets/configuration, the Compose files and deployment metadata, and the exact image digests. Without the digest you cannot reproduce the running artifact after a registry change.

Define RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long recovery may take). Backup frequency follows RPO; restore drills validate RTO.

sections.code:
# Database-consistent backup
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U app -d app \
  | gzip > "backups/app-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).sql.gz"

# Volume backup for non-database state
docker run --rm -v acme_pgdata:/data:ro -v "$PWD/backups":/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date +%Y%m%d).tgz -C /data .

# Restore drill into a throwaway database
gunzip -c backups/app-20260101.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T db psql -U app -d app_restore
sections.note: `-T` disables TTY allocation so the pipeline works in scripts.

sections.title: A backup stored on the same host is not disaster recovery
sections.body: Replicate off-host and test a restore that does not depend on the failed machine.

exercises.title: Backup script
exercises.prompt: Write a pg_dump backup piped to gzip with a timestamp.
exercises.expected: docker compose exec -T db pg_dump ... | gzip > backups/app-DATE.sql.gz

exercises.title: Restore drill
exercises.prompt: Restore into a separate database and run a sanity query.
exercises.expected: psql -d app_restore then SELECT count(*) from a core table.

questions.question: Why record image digests?
options: To reproduce the exact artifact later
